title: If these are powers, Jesus is stronger
source_text: Ἐβουλόμην δὲ πρὸς τὸν οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως τοιαῦτα λέγοντα τοιαῦτά τινα πρεπόντως αὐτῷ ἀδολεσχῆσαι· ἆρ᾿ οὖν οὐδέν εἰσιν οὗτοι, οὓς κατέλεξας, καὶ οὐδεμία δύναμίς ἐστιν ἐν Λεβαδίᾳ κατὰ τὸν Τροφώνιον οὐδ᾿ ἐν Θήβαις περὶ τὸν τοῦ Ἀμφιάρεω νεὼν οὐδ᾿ ἐν Ἀκαρνανίᾳ περὶ τὸν Ἀμφίλοχον οὐδ᾿ ἐν Κιλικίᾳ περὶ τὸν Μόψον; ἢ ἐστί τις ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις εἴτε δαίμων εἴτε ἥρως εἴτε καὶ θεὸς, ἐνεργῶν τινα μείζονα ἢ κατὰ ἄνθρωπον; εἰ μὲν γάρ φησι μηδὲν ἕτερον εἶναι μήτε δαιμόνιον μήτε θεῖον περὶ τούτους, κἂν νῦν ὁμολογησάτω τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην. Ἐπικούρειος ὢν καὶ μὴ τὰ αὐτὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησι φρονῶν καὶ μήτε δαίμονας γινώσκων μήτε κἂν ὡς Ἕλληνες θεοὺς σέβων, καὶ ἐλεγχέσθω ὅτι μάτην καὶ τὰ προειρημένα ὡς παραδεξάμενος αὐτὰ εἶναι ἀληθῆ ἐκόμισε καὶ τὰ ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς ἐπιφερόμενα. εἰ δὲ φήσει εἴτε δαίμονας εἴτε ἥρωας εἴτε καὶ θεοὺς εἶναι τοὺς κατειλεγμένους, ὁράτω ὅτι ὅπερ οὐ βούλεται κατασκευάσει δι᾿ ὧν εἴρηκεν, ὡς καὶ ὁ Ἰησοῦς τοιοῦτόν τι ἦν· διὸ καὶ δεδύνηται ἑαυτὸν παραστῆσαι οὐκ ὀλίγοις τῶν ἀνθρώπων θεόθεν ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἅπαξ δὲ τοῦτ᾿ ἐὰν παραδέξηται, ὅρα εἰ μὴ ἀναγκασθήσεται ἰσχυρότερον αὐτὸν φῆσαι τούτων. οἷς αὐτὸν συγκατηρίθμησεν· ἐπεὶ ἐκείνων μέν γε οὐδεὶς κωλύει τὰς πρὸς τοὺς ἑτέρους τιμὰς, οὗτος δὲ ἑαυτῷ θαῤῥῶν ὡς πάντων ἐκείνων δυνατώτερος ἀπαγορεύει τὰς τούτων ἀποδοχὰς ὡς μοχθηρῶν δαιμόνων καὶ τόπους „ἐπὶ γῆς προκατειληφότων. ἐπεὶ τῆς καθαρωτέρας οὐ δύνανται ἐφάψασθαι χώρας καὶ θειοτέρας, ἔνθα μὴ φθάνουσιν αἱ ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ μυρίων κακῶν παχύτητες.
pass_a_gloss: I wished (βούλομαι) to the one who I know not how (οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως) says such things to chatter (ἀδολεσχέω) some such things fittingly (πρεπόντως) to him: then (ἆρ᾿ οὖν) are these whom you listed (καταλέγω) nothing, and is there no power (δύναμις) in Lebadea at Trophonius, nor in Thebes about the temple (νεώς) of Amphiaraus, nor in Acarnania about Amphilochus, nor in Cilicia about Mopsus? Or is there in such some [one], whether demon (δαίμων) or hero (ἥρως) or even god, working (ἐνεργέω) some things greater than according to man? For if he says nothing else to be, neither demonic (δαιμόνιον) nor divine (θεῖον), about these, even now (κἂν νῦν) let him confess (ὁμολογέω) his own opinion (γνώμη), being an Epicurean (Ἐπικούρειος) and not thinking (φρονέω) the same as the Greeks, and neither knowing/recognising (γινώσκω) demons nor even as Greeks revering (σέβω) gods; and let him be refuted (ἐλέγχω) that in vain (μάτην) both the things said before (προειρημένα), as having accepted (παραδέχομαι) them to be true, he brought (κομίζω), and the things brought on (ἐπιφέρω) in what follows. But if he says that those listed are either demons or heroes or even gods, let him see that what he does not want he will establish (κατασκευάζω) through what he has said, that Jesus too was some such thing; wherefore he has also been able (δύναμαι) to present (παρίστημι) himself to not a few men to have come to dwell (ἐπιδημέω) from God (θεόθεν) for the race of men. And once (ἅπαξ) if he accepts this, see whether he will not be compelled (ἀναγκάζω) to say him stronger (ἰσχυρότερος) than those with whom he counted him (συγκαταριθμέω); since of those none forbids (κωλύω) the honours (τιμαί) toward the others, but this one, confident (θαρρέω) in himself as more powerful (δυνατώτερος) than all those, forbids (ἀπαγορεύω) the acceptances (ἀποδοχαί) of these as of wicked (μοχθηροί) demons and having occupied beforehand (προκαταλαμβάνω) places on earth, since they cannot touch (ἐφάπτομαι) the purer (καθαρωτέρα) and more divine region (χώρα), where the grossnesses (παχύτητες) from the earth and the countless (μυρία) evils in it do not reach (φθάνω).
pass_b_english: I should like to chat a little with the man who somehow says such things, in some such words as these, as befits him: Are these whom you have listed nothing, then? Is there no power at Lebadea connected with Trophonius, nor at Thebes around the temple of Amphiaraus, nor in Acarnania connected with Amphilochus, nor in Cilicia with Mopsus? Or is there in such places some being, whether a demon or a hero or even a god, working things greater than man can?

For if he says that there is nothing else about these, neither demonic nor divine, then let him at least now admit his own view as an Epicurean, one who does not think as the Greeks do, and who neither recognises demons nor even worships gods as the Greeks do. And let him be convicted of having brought forward to no purpose both what he said before, as though he accepted it as true, and what he goes on to add.

But if he says that those he lists are demons or heroes or even gods, let him see that by what he has said he will establish what he does not want: that Jesus too was something of this kind. That is why he has also been able to convince no small number of people that he came from God to dwell among the human race. And once Celsus admits this, see whether he will not be forced to say that Jesus is stronger than those with whom he has counted him. For none of those forbids the honours paid to the others; but Jesus, confident in himself as more powerful than all of them, forbids the acceptance of them as wicked demons, which have seized beforehand places on earth because they cannot touch the purer and more divine region, where the grossness that comes from the earth and from its countless evils does not reach.

choices.choice: Copy-text: staged source_3.json section 35 (Koetschau 3.35). ‘ἀδολεσχῆσαι’ (to chatter, talk idly) is Origen’s playful word for the imagined exchange; rendered ‘chat a little’; ‘τοιαῦτά τινα’ (some such things) rendered ‘in some such words as these’; ‘κατὰ τὸν Τροφώνιον’ rendered ‘connected with Trophonius’. ‘ἐβουλόμην’ (imperfect of wish) rendered ‘I should like’. The imagined questions are addressed to Celsus in the second person (‘οὓς κατέλεξας’, whom you have listed) and then Origen returns to the third person; both kept. ‘κἂν νῦν ὁμολογησάτω τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην, Ἐπικούρειος ὤν’ rendered ‘let him at least now admit his own view as an Epicurean’; the participle ‘ὤν’ is circumstantial and is kept so (Origen elsewhere suspects Celsus of being an Epicurean). ‘μήτε κἂν ὡς Ἕλληνες θεοὺς σέβων’ = ‘nor even worshipping gods as the Greeks do’. ‘θεόθεν ἐπιδεδημηκέναι τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων’ rendered ‘came from God to dwell among the human race’ (ἐπιδημέω = to come to stay, to visit); ‘ἑαυτὸν παραστῆσαι’ with the infinitive rendered ‘convince … that he came’. The subjects ‘αὐτόν’/‘οὗτος’ in the final sentences refer to Jesus; the English names him (‘that Jesus is stronger’, ‘but Jesus’) to avoid confusion with Celsus, and names Celsus once (‘once Celsus admits this’) where the Greek subject of ‘παραδέξηται’ is Celsus. The staged text opens a quotation mark before ‘ἐπὶ γῆς προκατειληφότων’ and never closes it; this may be an editorial signal that the phrase echoes wording used elsewhere (compare the same verb ‘προκαταλαμβάνουσιν’ in 3.34, and the Platonic picture of a purer region above the earth’s murk, Phaedo 109b–111c), but its source is uncertain, so the phrase is not set in quotation marks and no source is cited inline.
